outline.title: Which XGBoost Regularizers Transfer to a Small Bag-of-Embeddings Text Classifier? In One Small AG News Setting, Column Dropout and EMA Lowered Validation Error; Group-L1 and a Long Schedule Showed No Consistent Effect
outline.question: For a small bag-of-embeddings classifier trained on a 10k-article AG News subset, which of three XGBoost-derived regularizers lowers validation top-1 error relative to a matched ablation: per-step vocabulary-column dropout, group-L1 on embedding rows, or shrinkage implemented as a low-lr long schedule with EMA weight averaging?
outline.nugget: In this setting, vocabulary-column dropout lowered validation error against the stock control on all three evaluated folds. Of shrinkage's two parts, EMA weight averaging lowered error against its no-EMA ablation on every evaluated fold, while the low-lr long schedule showed no consistent effect. Group-L1 on embedding rows showed no consistent effect.
contributions: On seed-fold pairs zero to two, the column-drop-only arm scored 12.0833 validation error (per fold 12.1875, 11.875, 12.1875). The unregularized control at the same configuration scored 13.7708 (13.9375, 13.5, 13.875), and its single-seed smoke run gave 13.9375. Column dropout was lower on every one of the three folds.

At the default lr and epoch budget with column dropout, saving EMA-averaged weights gave a five-seed error of 12.025 (11.75, 11.125, 11.875, 11.75, 13.625), against 12.55 (12.1875, 11.875, 12.1875, 12.6875, 13.8125) without averaging. EMA was lower on all five seed-fold pairs. The verify tier gave 11.5833 and the smoke run 11.75.

At the halved lr and doubled epoch budget with column dropout, EMA weights scored 11.8542 (11.9375, 11.625, 12.0; smoke 11.9375). The same schedule without EMA scored 12.125 (12.25, 11.6875, 12.4375; smoke 12.25). EMA was lower on each of the three folds.

The low-lr long schedule gave no consistent gain over the default schedule. With EMA, it scored 11.8875 over five seeds (11.9375, 11.625, 12.0, 10.8125, 13.0625) against 12.025 (11.75, 11.125, 11.875, 11.75, 13.625). It was higher on seeds zero to two and lower on seeds three and four. Without EMA, it scored 12.125 (12.25, 11.6875, 12.4375) against 12.0833 (12.1875, 11.875, 12.1875), which is mixed.

At the default schedule, adding weak group-L1 to column dropout left the five-seed mean unchanged: 12.55 with the penalty and 12.55 without it. Per-seed values differed only at seed one (11.9375 vs 11.875) and seed four (13.75 vs 13.8125). The verify tier gave 12.1042 with the penalty and 12.0833 without it. The smoke runs of both arms gave 12.1875.

On top of the long-schedule EMA recipe (11.8542; per fold 11.9375, 11.625, 12.0), dense group-L1 scored 11.875 (12.0, 11.6875, 11.9375; smoke 12.0). Lazy group-L1 on batch-active rows at a larger coefficient scored 11.9375 (12.1875, 11.75, 11.875; smoke 12.1875). Neither penalty lowered error consistently across the three folds.
Two implementations of the long-schedule EMA recipe produced identical per-seed errors: verify 11.8542 in both, and five-seed 11.8875 in both. They differ only in the EMA decay cap.

sections.heading: Abstract
sections.purpose: State the question and how the study answers it: three XGBoost-derived mechanisms transferred to a hashed bag-of-embeddings model and compared against matched ablations on validation folds. Give the scoped headline. Column dropout and EMA lowered error on every evaluated fold. Group-L1 and the long schedule showed no consistent effect. The column-dropout result rests on three folds against an untuned control.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.purpose: State the task: AG News topic classification with a hashed mean-of-embeddings model. Frame the gap in related_xgboost's own wording. Column subsampling, L1-style penalties and shrinkage come from tree boosting, and XGBoost reports no text benchmarks. This study transfers column subsampling and shrinkage, adds a group-L1 analogue, and ablates each one separately. Make no novelty claim about prior text analogues. Then give the headline evidence and the contribution bullets, each scoped to this setting.

sections.heading: Related Work
sections.purpose: Group prior work by mechanism, giving for each how this study differs and where it falls short. The first group is tree-boosting regularization, the source of the transferred mechanisms. The second is fair-comparison and baseline-tuning methodology, which bears on our untuned control. The third is width as capacity control, which this study does not isolate.

sections.heading: Setup
sections.purpose: Give enough to reimplement. Cover the frozen scorer, the data, tokenization and hashing, the model and the loss. State the folds and the seed-fold pairing, and give the metric with its direction (lower error is better). List the default hyperparameters, the run tiers, the fixed step counts and the full run inventory. Then give each arm's configuration, including the column-dropout mask and the EMA decay schedule.

sections.heading: Results: Column Dropout
sections.purpose: Test whether vocabulary-column dropout lowers validation error against the stock control on matched seed-fold pairs zero to two. Then report the full-tier column-drop configurations, which differ in both drop rate and group-L1 and show no consistent ordering between them.

sections.heading: Results: Shrinkage (EMA and Long Schedule)
sections.purpose: Split shrinkage into its two parts. First test EMA averaging against its no-EMA ablation at the default schedule (five folds) and at the long schedule (three folds). Then test the low-lr long schedule against the default schedule, where the effect is mixed. Note that the no-EMA pair is the clean schedule-only contrast.

sections.heading: Results: Group-L1 on Embedding Rows
sections.purpose: Test group-L1 at the default schedule and on top of the long-schedule EMA recipe, in dense and lazy variants. Neither shows a consistent effect. Report this as a null result, bounded by the coefficient range tried.

sections.heading: Results: Variance, Fold Difficulty and Uninterpretable Bundles
sections.purpose: Show that fold four had the highest error in every five-seed arm and inflates the five-seed spread. Report the high-capacity bundles as negative but unattributable results, because they confound several factors.

sections.heading: Discussion: What Governs the EMA Gain
sections.purpose: Separate what was measured from what was derived. Measured: two decay caps gave identical per-seed errors. Derived from configuration, not from logged steps: the cap never binds, so the warmup term sets a shorter averaging window than the nominal cap implies. Give hedged hypotheses for the group-L1 null.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.purpose: Tie each limitation to a scope boundary and say whether it undermines the core claims. Cover the three-fold control, seed-fold coupling, nested tiers and the absence of significance tests. Then single-article granularity and validation-only selection. Then the untuned control and the missing alternative regularizer, confounded configurations, the schedule-window confound, and the derived claim that the cap never binds. Finally the absence of mechanism measurements, the coefficient range, the confounded bundles, the incomparable baseline and the single-dataset scope.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.purpose: Restate the question and the scoped answer. In this setting, column dropout and EMA averaging lowered validation error, while group-L1 and the long schedule showed no consistent effect. Give the strongest evidence, the five-fold EMA comparison. Name one limitation, the three-fold untuned control. Propose one next step: an equal-budget comparison against tuned hidden dropout plus weight decay.

issues.issue: The title is writer-authored, not an approved statement, and it says more than the evidence. 'Group-L1 and Long Schedules Do Not' asserts a negative effect, but claim_group_l1_default_null, claim_group_l1_long_null and claim_schedule_null only support 'showed no consistent effect'. limit_12 also says the group-L1 null may come from coefficients that were too small. 'Help' has no scope, although the column-dropout result rests on three folds against an untuned control (limit_1, limit_7).
issues.suggestion: Reword to match the nugget, e.g. '…? In One Small AG News Setting, Column Dropout and EMA Lowered Validation Error; Group-L1 and a Long Schedule Showed No Consistent Effect'.

issues.target: Section 11 Conclusion: 'column dropout and EMA averaging transfer'
issues.issue: 'Transfer' is stronger and broader than claim_overall, which is scoped 'in this setting' to validation folds. limit_15 restricts scope to one dataset, one model and short budgets, and limit_7 says column dropout may be generic regularization rather than a word-specific effect.
issues.suggestion: Use claim_overall's own wording ('in this setting … lowered validation error on all evaluated folds') rather than 'transfer', and cite limit_15 next to it.

issues.target: Section 6: claim_schedule_null used to 'separate shrinkage into its two parts'
issues.issue: The with-EMA schedule comparison also changes the averaging window and the step count (limit_10), so it does not isolate the schedule. Only the no-EMA pair is a schedule-only contrast. Without limit_10 in this section, readers may read the five-seed with-EMA contrast as a clean schedule test.
issues.suggestion: Add limit_10 to Section 6's evidence and state that the no-EMA pair is the schedule-only contrast. Also add limit_5 here, since one of the three long-schedule EMA margins is a single article.

issues.issue: The bullet presents 'the cap never binds' as a finding. limit_9 states this is derived from fold size, batch size and epochs, not measured, because step counts were not logged.
issues.suggestion: Either drop this bullet from the contributions and keep it in Section 9, or place limit_9 immediately next to it so the bullet is visibly marked as a derivation.

issues.issue: The headline result rests on a three-fold control with no five-seed run (limit_1), and the control is untuned (limit_7). Both appear only in Limitations. claim_coldrop_l1_vs_control is also not a matched ablation (scope_method).
issues.suggestion: Cite limit_1 and limit_7 in Section 5, and label the column-drop plus group-L1 versus control comparison as unmatched.

issues.issue: The bundles are called 'unattributable' here, but limit_13, which supports that label and gives the warmup confound for Bundle A, is cited only in Limitations.
issues.suggestion: Add limit_13 to Section 8's evidence.

issues.issue: The abstract plan lists the headline findings without any scope caveat: three-fold control, validation-only, one dataset.
issues.suggestion: Include limit_1 or limit_15 among the abstract's evidence so the selling points carry their scope.

issues.issue: The plan says XGBoost's regularizers 'have no tested analogue for neural bag-of-embeddings text models.' No approved statement supports this novelty claim. related_xgboost says only that XGBoost reports no text benchmarks and that this study transfers the mechanisms. The claim is also likely false, since input word/token dropout is established. It adds an unsupported scientific claim to the paper.
issues.suggestion: Drop the novelty claim. Frame the gap with related_xgboost's own wording: XGBoost reports no text benchmarks, and this study transfers column subsampling and shrinkage and adds a group-L1 analogue, ablating each one separately.

issues.issue: 'Group-L1 and Long Schedules Do Not' reads as a general negative. The evidence (claim_overall, claim_group_l1_*_null, claim_schedule_null) says only 'no consistent effect' at the tested coefficients and budgets. limit_12 leaves open that the group-L1 coefficients were simply too small.
issues.suggestion: Hedge the title to match the nugget, e.g. '...Column Dropout and EMA Help; Group-L1 and Long Schedules Show No Consistent Effect'.

issues.issue: A derived, unmeasured mechanism is listed as a contribution next to measured results, with no caveat. limit_9 states that step counts were not logged and that the non-binding cap is derived. The bullet as placed reads as a measured finding.
issues.suggestion: Either replace this bullet with claim_ema_cap_identity, which is the measured part, or place limit_9 directly beside it so readers see that the mechanism is derived.

issues.issue: The schedule-null comparison with EMA is confounded by the averaging window (limit_10). The long-schedule EMA margin at fold one is a single article (limit_5). Both caveats appear only in Limitations, so the results section overstates how clean the contrasts are.
issues.suggestion: Cite limit_10 and limit_5 in Section 6. Name the no-EMA pair as the schedule-only contrast, and name the five-fold default-schedule EMA result as the one carrying most of the weight.

issues.issue: claim_full_tier_coldrop compares configurations that differ in both drop rate and group-L1. claim_coldrop_l1_vs_control is not a matched ablation (scope_method). Neither caveat is cited where the result is reported.
issues.suggestion: Add limit_8 to Section 5. State that only the column-drop-only vs control comparison is matched. Add a transition explaining why the full-tier configurations matter: the five-seed spread, which leads into Section 8.

issues.issue: The fold-four finding needs limit_2, the seed-fold coupling. The bundles need limit_13 and the missing mask fallback from setup_mask, which is a competing explanation. Without these, 'negative but unattributable' is asserted rather than shown. The section also mixes two unrelated topics.
issues.suggestion: Cite limit_2, limit_13 and setup_mask in Section 8. Consider splitting the bundles into a short separate subsection, or moving them to an appendix-style paragraph, since they do not serve the nugget.

issues.issue: The section is titled 'What Governs the EMA Gain' but also carries the group-L1 hypotheses (limit_12). This splits its focus, and the group-L1 caveat ends up far from the group-L1 results.
issues.suggestion: Move limit_12 into Section 7, or rename Section 9 to cover both topics.

issues.issue: 'Column dropout and EMA averaging transfer' should keep the scope qualifiers: one dataset subset, validation folds only, an untuned control. Without them it reads as broader than the evidence.
issues.suggestion: Add scope wording from limit_15 and limit_6 alongside limit_1 and limit_7.

issues.issue: 'Group-L1 and Long Schedules Do Not' says more than the evidence. claim_overall and claim_group_l1_long_null only say these showed 'no consistent effect' on 3–5 folds. limit_12 adds that the group-L1 coefficients may have been too small, and limit_10 that the with-EMA schedule contrast is confounded. 'Help' for column dropout also rests on three folds against an untuned control (limit_1, limit_7).
issues.suggestion: Retitle using the hedge in the approved text, for example '... Column Dropout and EMA Lower Validation Error; Group-L1 and Long Schedules Show No Consistent Effect', or use a question-only title.

issues.target: Section 2 (Introduction): 'XGBoost's regularizers ... have no tested analogue for neural bag-of-embeddings text models'
issues.issue: This novelty claim is in no approved statement. related_xgboost only says XGBoost reports no text benchmarks and that this study transfers the mechanisms. The plan introduces an unsupported literature claim.
issues.suggestion: Frame the challenge with related_xgboost's own wording: the mechanisms come from tree boosting, which reports no text benchmarks, and this study transfers them. Drop 'no tested analogue'.

issues.issue: Listing 'The cap never binds' as a contribution presents a derived, unmeasured mechanism as a finding. limit_9 states that step counts were not logged and that the non-binding cap is derived, not measured. Section 9 separates measured from derived, but the contribution list does not, so it misleads.
issues.suggestion: Either replace this bullet with claim_ema_cap_identity, which is the measured fact, and leave the mechanism to Section 9, or keep it only where limit_9 sits beside it.

issues.issue: claim_highcap_bundles is reported without limit_13 or scope_method, the statements that make the bundles 'uninterpretable'. Read alone, the per-fold comparison against the default-capacity arms suggests capacity hurts.
issues.suggestion: Add limit_13, and the scope_method sentence on uninterpretable bundles, to Section 8's evidence, placed directly after the numbers.

issues.issue: limit_10 is the key caveat for claim_schedule_null: the with-EMA contrast changes the averaging window and step count, so only the no-EMA pair is schedule-only. It currently appears only in Limitations. limit_5, that the fold-one long-schedule EMA margin is a single article, likewise belongs beside claim_ema_long.
issues.suggestion: Cite limit_10 and limit_5 in Section 6 next to the claims they qualify.

issues.issue: claim_coldrop_l1_vs_control and claim_full_tier_coldrop involve the two non-matched comparisons that scope_method names, but limit_8, on drop rate and group-L1 changed together, is not cited here.
issues.suggestion: Cite limit_8, and limit_1 for the three-fold control, in Section 5.

issues.issue: claim_fold_four reports five-seed stds, but the seed-fold coupling that explains them (limit_2) is cited only in Limitations.
issues.suggestion: Cite limit_2 in Section 8. Consider a table with per-fold values and std for every arm, so that the spread is visible across all arms.

issues.issue: The abstract states that column dropout lowers error 'on every evaluated fold' without saying that only three folds were evaluated against an untuned, default-configuration control. The planned tuned alternative regularizer was never run.
issues.suggestion: Add limit_1 and limit_7 (or related_single_baseline) to the abstract's evidence, so that the scope of the headline is explicit.

issues.target: Section 11 (Conclusion): 'column dropout and EMA averaging transfer'
issues.issue: 'Transfer' implies a word-specific mechanism, which limit_7 and limit_11 leave untested: column dropout may act as generic regularization.
issues.suggestion: Phrase the conclusion as 'lowered validation error in this setting' and keep the claim_overall wording.

Derived from configuration, not from logged steps: the cap never binds, so the warmup term sets a shorter averaging window than the nominal cap implies. Give hedged hypotheses for the group-L1 null.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.purpose: Tie each limitation to a scope boundary and say whether it undermines the core claims. Cover the three-fold control, seed-fold coupling, nested tiers and the absence of significance tests. Then single-article granularity and validation-only selection. Then the untuned control and the missing alternative regularizer, confounded configurations, the schedule-window confound, and the derived claim that the cap never binds. Finally the absence of mechanism measurements, the coefficient range, the confounded bundles, the incomparable baseline and the single-dataset scope.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.purpose: Restate the question and the scoped answer. In this setting, column dropout and EMA averaging lowered validation error, while group-L1 and the long schedule showed no consistent effect. Give the strongest evidence, the five-fold EMA comparison. Name one limitation, the three-fold untuned control. Propose one next step: an equal-budget comparison against tuned hidden dropout plus weight decay.

points.claim: For a small bag-of-embeddings classifier trained on a 10k-article AG News subset, which of three XGBoost-derived regularizers lowers validation top-1 error relative to a matched ablation: per-step vocabulary-column dropout, group-L1 on embedding rows, or shrinkage implemented as a low-lr long schedule with EMA weight averaging?

In this setting, vocabulary-column dropout lowered validation error against the stock control on all three evaluated folds. Of shrinkage's two parts, EMA weight averaging lowered error against its no-EMA ablation on every evaluated fold, while the low-lr long schedule showed no consistent effect. Group-L1 on embedding rows showed no consistent effect.

On seed-fold pairs zero to two, the column-drop-only arm scored 12.0833 validation error (per fold 12.1875, 11.875, 12.1875). The unregularized control at the same configuration scored 13.7708 (13.9375, 13.5, 13.875), and its single-seed smoke run gave 13.9375. Column dropout was lower on every one of the three folds.

At the default lr and epoch budget with column dropout, saving EMA-averaged weights gave a five-seed error of 12.025 (11.75, 11.125, 11.875, 11.75, 13.625), against 12.55 (12.1875, 11.875, 12.1875, 12.6875, 13.8125) without averaging. EMA was lower on all five seed-fold pairs. The verify tier gave 11.5833 and the smoke run 11.75.
The unregularized control ran only on seed-fold pairs zero to two. The column-dropout effect therefore rests on three folds, and no five-seed control exists.

This study transfers column subsampling and shrinkage to a neural bag-of-embeddings model and adds group-L1 on embedding rows as its own L1-style analogue, ablating each separately.

A frozen scorer defines the data, the hashed-token mean-of-embeddings model and validation top-1 error; only the training script is edited. Arms add transferred mechanisms to the stock script. Most comparisons pair an arm with an ablation that removes one mechanism, at the same configuration and seed-fold pairs. Two comparisons do not: column dropout plus group-L1 against the stock control, and two column-drop configurations that differ in both drop rate and group-L1. Runs proceed through smoke, verify and full tiers, and later tiers reuse earlier seeds. Two high-capacity bundles without matched controls are reported as uninterpretable. Data are a class-stratified AG News subset built from the Hugging Face copy fancyzhx/ag_news with sampling seed 0: 8,000 training-split articles form the cross-validation pool, and 2,000 official-test articles form a held-out test set.
Text is lower-cased, split on non-alphanumerics and truncated to 64 tokens. Each token is hashed with crc32 modulo 20000, plus 1, into 20,000 buckets, with id 0 as padding.
The frozen model averages non-padding token embeddings, applies depth ReLU hidden layers of width hidden, and outputs 4 class logits.
Every arm trains with cross-entropy loss on the class logits; group-L1, where present, is added to this loss.

The pool is cut into 5 stratified folds by StratifiedKFold with shuffling and random_state 0. A run with seed i trains on the remaining folds and is scored on validation fold i, so seeds and folds are paired.
The metric is top-1 error in percent on the validation fold, and lower is better. No run scored the held-out test split.
The default configuration is lr 0.003, embed_dim 64, hidden 64, depth 1, weight_decay 0.0001 and 8 epochs. It uses Adam with coupled weight decay, batch 128 and normal initialisation with std 0.1.
Smoke runs use one seed with a 120-second budget, verify runs three seeds with 300 seconds, and full runs five seeds with 900 seconds. Later tiers reuse earlier seeds.
Each run trains on four of the five folds of the pool with batch 128 for 8 or 16 epochs, so the optimizer step count is fixed by the configuration.

Thirty registered runs over twelve candidate configurations all completed with a recorded validation score; none failed or were excluded. Twelve are smoke runs, twelve are verify runs and six are full-tier runs.
The control arm runs the unmodified training script at the default configuration, with no column dropout, group-L1 or averaging.

Column dropout draws one Bernoulli keep mask over the vocabulary per step, shared across the batch, and maps dropped ids to padding id 0. A row that would be fully masked keeps its original ids. The two high-capacity bundles lack this fallback.
The column-drop-only arm uses the same code with drop fraction p=0.4 and group-L1 coefficient 0.
The column-drop plus group-L1 arm uses drop rate 0.25 at each step and adds group-L1 at 1e-5 on the sum of embedding-row L2 norms, excluding the padding row.
The column-drop plus weak group-L1 arm uses drop fraction p=0.4 with group-L1 at 1e-6.
The EMA arm adds weight averaging to the column-drop-only arm with decay min(0.999, (1+t)/(10+t)) at step t and saves the EMA weights.

The long-schedule EMA arm uses lr 0.0015, 16 epochs, drop fraction p=0.4 and group-L1 0. Both implementations use EMA decay min(cap, (1+t)/(10+t)), the same warmup form as the default-schedule EMA arm, with cap 0.999 in one and 0.995 in the other, and save the EMA weights.
The long-schedule no-EMA arm uses lr 0.0015, 16 epochs, drop fraction p=0.4 and group-L1 0, and saves raw final weights.

Two group-L1 arms keep the long-schedule EMA recipe (lr 0.0015, 16 epochs, p=0.4, warmup EMA capped at 0.999). One adds dense group-L1 at 1e-5 on all non-padding embedding rows. The other adds lazy group-L1 at 1e-4 only on rows active in each batch.
High-capacity bundle A uses embed_dim 128, hidden 128, depth 2, lr 0.0015, weight_decay 5e-05 and 16 epochs. It adds column dropout p=0.3, group-L1 1e-5 and EMA at decay 0.999 without warmup.
High-capacity bundle B uses the same configuration with column dropout p=0.25, group-L1 1e-5 and EMA decay 0.999 with warmup.

On seed-fold pairs zero to two, the column-drop-only arm scored 12.0833 validation error (per fold 12.1875, 11.875, 12.1875). The unregularized control at the same configuration scored 13.7708 (13.9375, 13.5, 13.875), and its single-seed smoke run gave 13.9375. Column dropout was lower on every one of the three folds.

On the same three seed-fold pairs, the column-drop plus group-L1 arm scored 12.3542 (per fold 13.0625, 12.0, 12.0), and its smoke run gave 13.0625. The control scored 13.7708 (13.9375, 13.5, 13.875), so this arm was also lower on every fold.

Over five seed-fold pairs, the column-drop plus group-L1 arm scored 12.6875 (std 0.6673; per seed 13.0625, 12.0, 12.0, 12.875, 13.5). The column-drop-only arm scored 12.55 (std 0.7634; 12.1875, 11.875, 12.1875, 12.6875, 13.8125). The column-drop plus weak group-L1 arm scored 12.55 (std 0.724). The first two column-drop configurations, which differ in both drop rate and group-L1, showed no consistent ordering across seeds.

At the default lr and epoch budget with column dropout, saving EMA-averaged weights gave a five-seed error of 12.025 (11.75, 11.125, 11.875, 11.75, 13.625), against 12.55 (12.1875, 11.875, 12.1875, 12.6875, 13.8125) without averaging. EMA was lower on all five seed-fold pairs. The verify tier gave 11.5833 and the smoke run 11.75.

At the halved lr and doubled epoch budget with column dropout, EMA weights scored 11.8542 (11.9375, 11.625, 12.0; smoke 11.9375). The same schedule without EMA scored 12.125 (12.25, 11.6875, 12.4375; smoke 12.25). EMA was lower on each of the three folds.

The low-lr long schedule gave no consistent gain over the default schedule. With EMA, it scored 11.8875 over five seeds (11.9375, 11.625, 12.0, 10.8125, 13.0625) against 12.025 (11.75, 11.125, 11.875, 11.75, 13.625). It was higher on seeds zero to two and lower on seeds three and four. Without EMA, it scored 12.125 (12.25, 11.6875, 12.4375) against 12.0833 (12.1875, 11.875, 12.1875), which is mixed.

Under the warmup EMA, the averaging window grows with step count, so the with-EMA schedule comparison changes the averaging window and doubles the steps along with lr and epochs. The no-EMA pair, long schedule against the column-drop-only arm, is the schedule-only contrast.

At the default schedule, adding weak group-L1 to column dropout left the five-seed mean unchanged: 12.55 with the penalty and 12.55 without it. Per-seed values differed only at seed one (11.9375 vs 11.875) and seed four (13.75 vs 13.8125). The verify tier gave 12.1042 with the penalty and 12.0833 without it. The smoke runs of both arms gave 12.1875.

On top of the long-schedule EMA recipe (11.8542; per fold 11.9375, 11.625, 12.0), dense group-L1 scored 11.875 (12.0, 11.6875, 11.9375; smoke 12.0). Lazy group-L1 on batch-active rows at a larger coefficient scored 11.9375 (12.1875, 11.75, 11.875; smoke 12.1875). Neither penalty lowered error consistently across the three folds.
The group-L1 null may reflect coefficients too small relative to the coupled Adam weight decay, or Adam rescaling the penalty. Neither possibility was checked.

points.claim: In every five-seed arm, the seed-four/fold-four pair had the highest error: 13.5, 13.8125, 13.75, 13.625 and 13.0625. Each five-seed std (0.6673, 0.7634, 0.724, 0.9412, 0.8094) exceeds the three-seed std of the same arm on seeds zero to two.

Two bundles that doubled width, used depth two and combined all three mechanisms scored above both default-capacity column-drop arms on every one of folds zero to two. Bundle A, averaging without warmup, scored 14.5417 (16.1875, 13.3125, 14.125; smoke 16.1875). Bundle B, with warmup, scored 13.3125 (13.9375, 12.5625, 13.4375; smoke 13.9375). The column-drop plus group-L1 arm scored 12.3542 (13.0625, 12.0, 12.0) and the column-drop-only arm 12.0833 (12.1875, 11.875, 12.1875).

The high-capacity bundles confound capacity, lr, epochs, drop rate and EMA variant, and no capacity-matched control ran, so neither result can be attributed to any mechanism. One averaged from initialisation without warmup, a competing explanation for its high error.

sections.heading: Discussion: What Governs the EMA Gain

points.claim: Two implementations of the long-schedule EMA recipe produced identical per-seed errors: verify 11.8542 in both, and five-seed 11.8875 in both. They differ only in the EMA decay cap.

The cap never binds in these runs. The step count is fixed by the recorded pool size, the five-fold split, the batch size and the epoch budget, and at that step count the warmup term of the decay schedule stays below either cap for the whole run. The averaging that helped is therefore governed by the warmup schedule, whose effective window is shorter than the nominal cap implies.

EMA effects are compared across separate runs, not as raw versus averaged weights from the same run. Step counts were not logged; the claim that the decay cap never binds is derived from the recorded fold size, batch size and epochs, not measured.

No mechanism measurements were taken: no train/validation gap, learning curves, per-token reliance or embedding-row norms. Two hypotheses remain untested: that gains are early stopping in disguise, and that dropout prevents reliance on topic tokens.
The unregularized control ran only on seed-fold pairs zero to two. The column-dropout effect therefore rests on three folds, and no five-seed control exists.
Seed index and validation fold are coupled, so seed variance mixes initialisation noise with fold difficulty. Fold four is consistently hardest.
Verify and full tiers reuse the seeds of earlier tiers. They are nested subsets, not independent replicates.
Each comparison is a sign pattern over three or five folds. No significance test or confidence interval was computed.

Per-fold errors move in steps of one validation article. One of the three long-schedule EMA margins, at fold one, is a single article, so that comparison is weak on its own; the five-fold default-schedule EMA comparison carries most of the weight.
All arms were selected and compared on validation folds. The held-out test split was never scored, so selection bias toward validation noise is possible.

The planned comparison against hidden dropout plus weight decay, tuned with an equal trial budget, never ran. Column dropout may act as generic regularization rather than a word-specific effect. The control used the default configuration and was not tuned for its own arm.
The two default-schedule column-drop configurations change drop rate and group-L1 together. Dose-response in the drop rate was not measured.
The logistic-regression baseline quoted in the profile was never run under this protocol and is not directly comparable with any arm.

The EMA arm adds weight averaging to the column-drop-only arm with decay min(0.999, (1+t)/(10+t)) at step t and saves the EMA weights.

The long-schedule EMA arm uses lr 0.0015, 16 epochs, drop fraction p=0.4 and group-L1 0. Both implementations use EMA decay min(cap, (1+t)/(10+t)), the same warmup form as the default-schedule EMA arm, with cap 0.999 in one and 0.995 in the other, and save the EMA weights.
The long-schedule no-EMA arm uses lr 0.0015, 16 epochs, drop fraction p=0.4 and group-L1 0, and saves raw final weights.

Two group-L1 arms keep the long-schedule EMA recipe (lr 0.0015, 16 epochs, p=0.4, warmup EMA capped at 0.999). One adds dense group-L1 at 1e-5 on all non-padding embedding rows. The other adds lazy group-L1 at 1e-4 only on rows active in each batch.
High-capacity bundle A uses embed_dim 128, hidden 128, depth 2, lr 0.0015, weight_decay 5e-05 and 16 epochs. It adds column dropout p=0.3, group-L1 1e-5 and EMA at decay 0.999 without warmup.
High-capacity bundle B uses the same configuration with column dropout p=0.25, group-L1 1e-5 and EMA decay 0.999 with warmup.

On seed-fold pairs zero to two, the column-drop-only arm scored 12.0833 validation error (per fold 12.1875, 11.875, 12.1875). The unregularized control at the same configuration scored 13.7708 (13.9375, 13.5, 13.875), and its single-seed smoke run gave 13.9375. Column dropout was lower on every one of the three folds.

On the same three seed-fold pairs, the column-drop plus group-L1 arm scored 12.3542 (per fold 13.0625, 12.0, 12.0), and its smoke run gave 13.0625. The control scored 13.7708 (13.9375, 13.5, 13.875), so this arm was also lower on every fold.

Over five seed-fold pairs, the column-drop plus group-L1 arm scored 12.6875 (std 0.6673; per seed 13.0625, 12.0, 12.0, 12.875, 13.5). The column-drop-only arm scored 12.55 (std 0.7634; 12.1875, 11.875, 12.1875, 12.6875, 13.8125). The column-drop plus weak group-L1 arm scored 12.55 (std 0.724). The first two column-drop configurations, which differ in both drop rate and group-L1, showed no consistent ordering across seeds.

At the default lr and epoch budget with column dropout, saving EMA-averaged weights gave a five-seed error of 12.025 (11.75, 11.125, 11.875, 11.75, 13.625), against 12.55 (12.1875, 11.875, 12.1875, 12.6875, 13.8125) without averaging. EMA was lower on all five seed-fold pairs. The verify tier gave 11.5833 and the smoke run 11.75.

At the halved lr and doubled epoch budget with column dropout, EMA weights scored 11.8542 (11.9375, 11.625, 12.0; smoke 11.9375). The same schedule without EMA scored 12.125 (12.25, 11.6875, 12.4375; smoke 12.25). EMA was lower on each of the three folds.

The low-lr long schedule gave no consistent gain over the default schedule. With EMA, it scored 11.8875 over five seeds (11.9375, 11.625, 12.0, 10.8125, 13.0625) against 12.025 (11.75, 11.125, 11.875, 11.75, 13.625). It was higher on seeds zero to two and lower on seeds three and four. Without EMA, it scored 12.125 (12.25, 11.6875, 12.4375) against 12.0833 (12.1875, 11.875, 12.1875), which is mixed.

Under the warmup EMA, the averaging window grows with step count, so the with-EMA schedule comparison changes the averaging window and doubles the steps along with lr and epochs. The no-EMA pair, long schedule against the column-drop-only arm, is the schedule-only contrast.

At the default schedule, adding weak group-L1 to column dropout left the five-seed mean unchanged: 12.55 with the penalty and 12.55 without it. Per-seed values differed only at seed one (11.9375 vs 11.875) and seed four (13.75 vs 13.8125). The verify tier gave 12.1042 with the penalty and 12.0833 without it. The smoke runs of both arms gave 12.1875.

On top of the long-schedule EMA recipe (11.8542; per fold 11.9375, 11.625, 12.0), dense group-L1 scored 11.875 (12.0, 11.6875, 11.9375; smoke 12.0). Lazy group-L1 on batch-active rows at a larger coefficient scored 11.9375 (12.1875, 11.75, 11.875; smoke 12.1875). Neither penalty lowered error consistently across the three folds.
The group-L1 null may reflect coefficients too small relative to the coupled Adam weight decay, or Adam rescaling the penalty. Neither possibility was checked.

points.claim: In every five-seed arm, the seed-four/fold-four pair had the highest error: 13.5, 13.8125, 13.75, 13.625 and 13.0625. Each five-seed std (0.6673, 0.7634, 0.724, 0.9412, 0.8094) exceeds the three-seed std of the same arm on seeds zero to two.

sections.heading: Discussion: What Governs the EMA Gain

points.claim: Two implementations of the long-schedule EMA recipe produced identical per-seed errors: verify 11.8542 in both, and five-seed 11.8875 in both. They differ only in the EMA decay cap.

The cap never binds in these runs. The step count is fixed by the recorded pool size, the five-fold split, the batch size and the epoch budget, and at that step count the warmup term of the decay schedule stays below either cap for the whole run. The averaging that helped is therefore governed by the warmup schedule, whose effective window is shorter than the nominal cap implies.

EMA effects are compared across separate runs, not as raw versus averaged weights from the same run. Step counts were not logged; the claim that the decay cap never binds is derived from the recorded fold size, batch size and epochs, not measured.

No mechanism measurements were taken: no train/validation gap, learning curves, per-token reliance or embedding-row norms. Two hypotheses remain untested: that gains are early stopping in disguise, and that dropout prevents reliance on topic tokens.
The unregularized control ran only on seed-fold pairs zero to two. The column-dropout effect therefore rests on three folds, and no five-seed control exists.
Seed index and validation fold are coupled, so seed variance mixes initialisation noise with fold difficulty. Fold four is consistently hardest.
Verify and full tiers reuse the seeds of earlier tiers. They are nested subsets, not independent replicates.
Each comparison is a sign pattern over three or five folds. No significance test or confidence interval was computed.

Per-fold errors move in steps of one validation article. One of the three long-schedule EMA margins, at fold one, is a single article, so that comparison is weak on its own; the five-fold default-schedule EMA comparison carries most of the weight.
All arms were selected and compared on validation folds. The held-out test split was never scored, so selection bias toward validation noise is possible.

The planned comparison against hidden dropout plus weight decay, tuned with an equal trial budget, never ran. Column dropout may act as generic regularization rather than a word-specific effect. The control used the default configuration and was not tuned for its own arm.
The two default-schedule column-drop configurations change drop rate and group-L1 together. Dose-response in the drop rate was not measured.
The logistic-regression baseline quoted in the profile was never run under this protocol and is not directly comparable with any arm.
Results cover one dataset subset, one small hashed-vocabulary model and short training budgets. Historical code provenance relies on recorded candidate source versions, not execution snapshots.

In this setting, vocabulary-column dropout lowered validation error against the stock control on all three evaluated folds. Of shrinkage's two parts, EMA weight averaging lowered error against its no-EMA ablation on every evaluated fold, while the low-lr long schedule showed no consistent effect. Group-L1 on embedding rows showed no consistent effect.

At the default lr and epoch budget with column dropout, saving EMA-averaged weights gave a five-seed error of 12.025 (11.75, 11.125, 11.875, 11.75, 13.625), against 12.55 (12.1875, 11.875, 12.1875, 12.6875, 13.8125) without averaging. EMA was lower on all five seed-fold pairs. The verify tier gave 11.5833 and the smoke run 11.75.
The unregularized control ran only on seed-fold pairs zero to two. The column-dropout effect therefore rests on three folds, and no five-seed control exists.

The planned comparison against hidden dropout plus weight decay, tuned with an equal trial budget, never ran. Column dropout may act as generic regularization rather than a word-specific effect. The control used the default configuration and was not tuned for its own arm.

sections.body: We ask which of three XGBoost-derived regularizers lowers validation top-1 error, relative to a matched ablation, for a small bag-of-embeddings classifier trained on a 10k-article AG News subset: per-step vocabulary-column dropout, group-L1 on embedding rows, or shrinkage implemented as a low-lr long schedule with EMA weight averaging [scope_question]. At the default lr and epoch budget with column dropout, saving EMA-averaged weights gave a five-seed error of 12.025 against 12.55 without averaging, and EMA was lower on all five seed-fold pairs [claim_ema_default]. sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body:
We study topic classification on AG News with a small bag-of-embeddings classifier trained on a 10k-article subset, and we ask which of three XGBoost-derived regularizers lowers validation top-1 error (lower is better) relative to a matched ablation: per-step vocabulary-column dropout, group-L1 on embedding rows, or shrinkage implemented as a low-lr long schedule with EMA weight averaging [scope_question].

These regularizers come from tree boosting: XGBoost is a scalable tree-boosting system whose regularized objective uses leaf-count and L2 leaf-weight penalties, alongside shrinkage and column subsampling, and it reports no text benchmarks [related_xgboost]. This study transfers column subsampling and shrinkage to a neural bag-of-embeddings model, adds group-L1 on embedding rows as its own L1-style analogue, and ablates each one separately [related_xgboost].

In this setting, vocabulary-column dropout lowered validation error against the stock control on all three evaluated folds, and group-L1 on embedding rows showed no consistent effect [claim_overall]. Of shrinkage's two parts, EMA weight averaging lowered error against its no-EMA ablation on every evaluated fold, while the low-lr long schedule showed no consistent effect [claim_overall].

Our first finding is that column dropout lowers error against the unregularized control: on seed-fold pairs zero to two, the column-drop-only arm scored 12.0833 validation error against 13.7708 for the control at the same configuration [claim_coldrop_vs_control]. Column dropout was lower on every one of the three folds [claim_coldrop_vs_control].

Our second finding isolates EMA within shrinkage: at the default lr and epoch budget with column dropout, saving EMA-averaged weights gave a five-seed error of 12.025 against 12.55 without averaging [claim_ema_default]. EMA was lower on all five seed-fold pairs [claim_ema_default].

Our third finding is a null result for group-L1: at the default schedule, adding weak group-L1 to column dropout left the five-seed mean unchanged at 12.55 with the penalty and 12.55 without it [claim_group_l1_default_null]. Per-seed values differed only at seed one and seed four [claim_group_l1_default_null].

sections.heading: Related Work
sections.body:
XGBoost is a scalable tree-boosting system whose regularized objective penalizes leaf count and L2 leaf weights, and it also uses shrinkage and column subsampling [related_xgboost] [arXiv:1603.02754]. The XGBoost paper reports no text benchmarks [related_xgboost]. This study transfers column subsampling and shrinkage to a neural bag-of-embeddings model [related_xgboost]. It also adds group-L1 on embedding rows as its own L1-style analogue and ablates each mechanism separately [related_xgboost].

Work on connectome-constrained circuit models shows that comparisons are biased when baselines are under-tuned or inherit parameters tuned for the favoured model, and it names the machine-learning analogues [related_tuning_bias] [arXiv:2611.14508v1]. By analogy, the same caution applies here, because our control shares an untuned default configuration with the treatments [related_tuning_bias]. A related study cautions against relying on a single, unjustified task-specific baseline [related_single_baseline] [arXiv:2611.14519v1]. Our control is likewise one default-configuration model, with no tuned alternative regularizer in its place [related_single_baseline].

MobileNets treats width multipliers as a capacity-accuracy trade-off in vision [related_width] [arXiv:1704.04861]. This study varied width only inside confounded high-capacity bundles, so it does not isolate capacity [related_width].

sections.heading: Setup
sections.body:
A frozen scorer defines the data, the hashed-token mean-of-embeddings model and validation top-1 error, and only the training script is edited [scope_method]. Each arm adds transferred mechanisms to the stock script [scope_method]. Most comparisons pair an arm with an ablation that removes one mechanism, at the same configuration and seed-fold pairs [scope_method]. Two comparisons lack this pairing: column dropout plus group-L1 against the stock control, and two column-drop configurations that differ in both drop rate and group-L1 [scope_method]. Runs proceed through smoke, verify and full tiers, and later tiers reuse earlier seeds [scope_method]. We report two high-capacity bundles without matched controls as uninterpretable [scope_method]. No arm was scored on the held-out test split [scope_method].

The data are a class-stratified AG News subset built from the Hugging Face copy fancyzhx/ag_news with sampling seed 0 [setup_data]. Of these articles, 8,000 from the training split form the cross-validation pool, and 2,000 from the official test split form a held-out test set [setup_data]. Text is lower-cased, split on non-alphanumerics and truncated to 64 tokens [setup_tokens]. Each token is hashed with crc32 modulo 20000, plus 1, into 20,000 buckets, with id 0 reserved for padding [setup_tokens].

The frozen model averages the non-padding token embeddings, applies depth ReLU hidden layers of width hidden, and outputs 4 class logits [setup_model]. Every arm trains with cross-entropy loss on the class logits, and group-L1, where present, is added to this loss [setup_loss].

The pool is cut into 5 stratified folds by StratifiedKFold with shuffling and random_state 0 [setup_folds]. A run with seed i trains on the remaining folds and is scored on validation fold i, so seeds and folds are paired [setup_folds]. The metric is top-1 error in percent on the validation fold, and lower is better [setup_metric]. No run scored the held-out test split [setup_metric].

The default configuration is lr 0.003, embed_dim 64, hidden 64, depth 1, weight_decay 0.0001 and 8 epochs [setup_default]. Training uses Adam with coupled weight decay, batch 128 and normal initialisation with std 0.1 [setup_default]. Smoke runs use one seed with a 120-second budget, verify runs use three seeds with 300 seconds, and full runs use five seeds with 900 seconds [setup_tiers]. Later tiers reuse the seeds of earlier tiers [setup_tiers]. Each run trains on four of the five folds of the pool with batch 128 for 8 or 16 epochs, so the configuration fixes the optimizer step count [setup_steps].

Thirty registered runs over twelve candidate configurations all completed with a recorded validation score, and none failed or were excluded [setup_runs]. Of these runs, twelve are smoke runs, twelve are verify runs and six are full-tier runs [setup_runs].

The control arm runs the unmodified training script at the default configuration, with no column dropout, group-L1 or averaging [setup_control]. Column dropout draws one Bernoulli keep mask over the vocabulary per step, shared across the batch, and maps dropped ids to padding id 0 [setup_mask]. A row that would be fully masked keeps its original ids [setup_mask]. The two high-capacity bundles lack this fallback [setup_mask].

The column-drop-only arm uses the same code with drop fraction p=0.4 and group-L1 coefficient 0 [setup_coldrop_only]. The column-drop plus group-L1 arm uses drop rate 0.25 at each step and adds group-L1 at 1e-5 on the sum of embedding-row L2 norms, excluding the padding row [setup_coldrop_l1]. The column-drop plus weak group-L1 arm uses drop fraction p=0.4 with group-L1 at 1e-6 [setup_coldrop_weak_l1].

The EMA arm adds weight averaging to the column-drop-only arm with decay min(0.999, (1+t)/(10+t)) at step t, and it saves the EMA weights [setup_ema]. The long-schedule EMA arm uses lr 0.0015, 16 epochs, drop fraction p=0.4 and group-L1 0 [setup_long_ema]. Its two implementations use EMA decay min(cap, (1+t)/(10+t)), the same warmup form as the default-schedule EMA arm, with cap 0.999 in one and 0.995 in the other, and both save the EMA weights [setup_long_ema]. The long-schedule no-EMA arm uses lr 0.0015, 16 epochs, drop fraction p=0.4 and group-L1 0, and it saves the raw final weights [setup_long_noema].

Two group-L1 arms keep the long-schedule EMA recipe (lr 0.0015, 16 epochs, p=0.4, warmup EMA capped at 0.999) [setup_long_l1]. One adds dense group-L1 at 1e-5 on all non-padding embedding rows [setup_long_l1]. The other adds lazy group-L1 at 1e-4 only on rows active in each batch [setup_long_l1].

High-capacity bundle A uses embed_dim 128, hidden 128, depth 2, lr 0.0015, weight_decay 5e-05 and 16 epochs [setup_highcap_a]. It adds column dropout p=0.3, group-L1 1e-5 and EMA at decay 0.999 without warmup [setup_highcap_a]. High-capacity bundle B uses the same configuration with column dropout p=0.25, group-L1 1e-5 and EMA decay 0.999 with warmup [setup_highcap_b].
